title: AI Data Center Growth Is Outpacing Compute Planning
summary: Get practical insight into AI data center growth and storage planning for AI infrastructure as training and inference records keep compounding.
body_text: August 14, 2026 8 min read Technology AI Data Center Growth Is Outpacing Compute Planning WD AI capacity planning will fail when it treats storage as a downstream detail instead of the system that carries state. Key Takeaways AI infrastructure planning needs to start with the data lifecycle because training, inference, retrieval, and audit workflows all create data that remains after compute cycles end. Storage economics shape what AI teams can retain, reuse, and evaluate, which makes cost per stored PB a strategic metric rather than a budget detail. Tiered architecture gives teams a practical way to match latency, durability, and cost to the value of each dataset over time. AI data center growth is now a storage planning problem as much as a GPU planning problem. IDC has projected that the total volume of global annual data generation will grow to 718ZB by 2030.* That scale changes how AI infrastructure should be funded, tiered, and governed. AI data growth now exceeds compute growth planning AI data continues to grow after the compute event has finished. A training run ends, an inference request completes, and a retrieval query returns an answer, but the system still holds logs, embeddings, checkpoints, traces, prompts, outputs, and evaluation sets. Capacity plans that only track GPU use miss the residue that becomes the operating record. A model team can run a short fine-tuning cycle and still retain source data, cleaned data, rejected samples, validation sets, model snapshots, and performance reports. Each stage creates a separate storage class with a different access pattern. Some data stays hot for active iteration, while other data becomes warm standby data or cold recordkeeping. The operational mistake is treating AI data storage as a byproduct. Data is the memory of the AI system. Your storage plan decides what can be reused, what must be recomputed, and what becomes too expensive to keep. Data is the memory of the AI system. AI inference creates persistent data long after compute cycles end Inference creates data every time a user, agent, or application calls a model. The visible answer is only one part of the output. Production inference also creates prompts, responses, routing records, safety traces, latency data, retrieval context, feedback signals, and records needed for audit or model refinement. A customer support assistant can produce a short answer while the platform stores the prompt, the retrieved documents, the model response, the policy check, and the user rating. At low volume, that looks manageable. At production volume, the record of inference becomes a growing data estate. This is where compute-centric planning breaks. GPU time is consumed in bursts, while inference data persists across product cycles. Teams that ignore this gap can end up compressing retention windows, weakening evaluation data, and creating blind spots in quality analysis. Training pipelines generate more retained data than expected Training storage requirements extend beyond the final dataset used for the model. Teams retain raw inputs, filtered versions, synthetic samples, tokenized data, checkpoints, experiment metadata, failed runs, and evaluation outputs. The storage footprint grows because training is an iterative pipeline, rather than a single dataset loaded once. A foundation model team working with text, audio, and video will keep multiple forms of the same source material. Raw media supports reprocessing, cleaned data supports training, embeddings support retrieval, and validation sets support regression testing. Deleting one layer can save capacity, but it also removes optionality. That tradeoff matters when model quality depends on repeated experimentation. If storage cost forces a team to discard data before its later value is known, the AI program can become less flexible. The cost can show up as slower iteration, repeated data preparation, and narrower evaluation coverage. Single-tier AI infrastructure breaks under exabyte-scale retention Single-tier storage works when the active dataset dominates the footprint. AI retention breaks that model because only a fraction of data needs the lowest latency at any given time. Checkpoints, inference records, synthetic data, and audit data belong on separate tiers with separate economics. An all-flash tier can support hot training windows, feature stores, and latency-sensitive retrieval. Capacity-optimized HDD storage can hold large retained datasets, warm objects, and long-lived records. Object storage can provide a practical control plane for lifecycle policy, metadata, and movement across access classes. The failure mode is economic first, then operational. When every dataset lands on the most expensive tier, teams will likely start deleting data to protect budgets. When data moves without policy, recovery slows and lineage breaks. Right tier, right workload functions as a storage architecture rule and a media-neutral design principle. AI data storage economics determine long-term infrastructure viability AI storage economics decide how long useful data can remain accessible without distorting the cost base. The relevant question is no longer only how much storage costs at deployment. The more useful question is how cost per stored PB behaves as data compounds across training, inference, RAG, fine-tuning, and compliance. Data center electricity consumption is projected to reach around 945TWh by 2030 . That pressure turns watts, racks, cooling, and floor space into storage economics alongside facilities planning. Retained data must fit the power budget as well as the capacity budget. Economic planning needs to separate these cost signals: Cost per stored PB across hot, warm, and cold data tiers Power use per retained dataset over its full lifecycle Recovery cost when rebuilds touch large retained pools Data movement cost between training and inference systems Margin exposure when retention expands faster than revenue The durable solution retains data according to value. Teams assign data to tiers based on access frequency, reuse value, and risk. WD fits this execution context through capacity-optimized HDD infrastructure that supports retained AI data where economics carry the most weight. Tiered AI infrastructure reduces rebuild risk at petabyte scale Tiered AI infrastructure lowers rebuild risk because it prevents every dataset from depending on the same performance and recovery assumptions. As data reaches petabyte scale, rebuild windows, replication overhead, and rebalancing traffic become system-level constraints. Storage tiers give architects more control over where durability, latency, and cost tradeoffs sit. A platform team can keep active model checkpoints near training clusters, move older checkpoints into lower-cost capacity storage, and retain audit records in a policy-governed object store. That pattern reduces pressure on hot tiers while keeping data available for reuse, investigation, or compliance review. Planning area What disciplined tiering clarifies Hot training data Active data stays close to GPU clusters so training jobs avoid unnecessary I/O delays. Warm reuse data Recently used datasets remain accessible without occupying the most expensive performance tier. Long-retention records Audit data and inference history can remain available without crowding active training pools. Recovery planning Rebuilds can be scoped by tier so failures avoid pushing every dataset through the same path. Cost control Storage spend maps to access value rather than treating all AI data as equally urgent. Tiering also makes failure behavior easier to strategize around. When access patterns are clear, teams can set replication, erasure coding, and movement policy with fewer exceptions. That discipline matters more as stored data becomes larger than any single training cycle. Data retention policies now shape model improvement speed Retention policy now affects model improvement speed because teams need past data to test, compare, and refine new versions. A narrow retention window can reduce storage cost, but it can also remove the evidence needed to diagnose regressions, tune retrieval, and evaluate new training recipes. A RAG system needs historical queries, retrieved passages, answer quality signals, and user feedback to improve retrieval accuracy. A safety team needs old prompts and outputs to test policy updates against prior failure cases. A data science team needs past validation sets to prove that a new model improves one metric without degrading another. The policy choice starts with classification, then sets tiering, compression, expiration, and protection according to reuse value. Strong retention policy gives teams a working memory. Weak retention policy makes each improvement cycle start with less evidence than the last. Storage as a procurement decision puts AI infrastructure planning at risk AI infrastructure planning can fail when storage is bought after compute , rather than designed with the data lifecycle. Procurement can solve a capacity shortfall. Architecture must solve accumulation, access, durability, power, recovery, and cost across years of training and inference use. The better operating model starts with data flows. What gets generated during training? What does inference retain? Which records support compliance? Which datasets must stay close to GPUs? Which data can move to capacity tiers without slowing iteration? Those answers shape the storage system before purchase orders are written. Disciplined execution is what separates scalable AI infrastructure from expensive capacity growth. Compute creates value in moments. Data carries the record of those moments. WD ’s role fits where that record must stay accessible, durable, and economically sustainable as AI systems keep producing more of it. * Source: IDC Global DataSphere Forecast, 2026–2030, June 2026, Document # US53425426 Artificial Intelligence Data Center Infrastructure Technology and Strategy

title: Business continuity for the modern contact center: Layered resilience for the next disruption
summary: Learn how layered business continuity strengthens contact centers with AI, automation, and resilient customer service.
body_text: Business continuity for the modern contact center: Layered resilience for the next disruption by Johnny Sun August 3, 2026 Share A severe storm makes landfall overnight. By morning, flight cancellations cascade, payment systems slow, and your digital channels start to wobble under load. In the contact center, queues spike before your first shift changes. Agents are asking whether they should evacuate, supervisors are trying to rebalance coverage, and customers are refreshing your app looking for answers you haven’t published yet. In moments like these, “business continuity” stops being a compliance artifact and becomes a test of trust. That’s why business continuity and disaster recovery (BCDR) can’t be treated as an IT-only concern. The contact center sits at the intersection of real-time customer anxiety, operational strain, and brand credibility. And the risk profile is changing fast. Impact: The disruption stack is getting taller and more concurrent In Contact Center Pipeline, Lou Corbeil ranked five threats that have become the persistent continuity pressure points for contact centers: cyberattacks, platform outages, severe weather/climate-driven events, workforce disruption, and vendor/telecom failures — with data sovereignty mandates emerging as an additional “rapid reroute” trigger. These aren’t theoretical categories. They compound. Climate volatility is broadening the blast radius. In the U.S. alone, NOAA reports 27 billion‑dollar weather/climate disasters in 2024 — a scale that forces enterprises to plan for regional simultaneity, not isolated events. Cyber disruption is expensive and operationally destabilizing. IBM reports the global average cost of a data breach reached $4.4 million, with disruption and post-incident response driving cost. The “human element” remains a dominant exposure point. Verizon’s 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) found the human element was a component of 60% of breaches , underscoring why workforce controls and governance are now continuity controls. Continuity is no longer about surviving a single outage. It’s about sustaining service while multiple failure modes activate across technology, people, and third parties. Continuity plans reduce customer anxiety, protect staff The most underappreciated continuity lever is not a redundant system. It’s reducing uncertainty . Corbeil notes that proactive incident communications can “significantly reduce customer anxiety and help manage volume.” That statement matters because it reframes communications as a load-management mechanism—not a PR afterthought. At the same time, automation changes the operating equation: When AI and automation absorb routine demand, the remaining agent-handled interactions are more likely to be high-value, emotionally charged, and urgent —making agent availability and safety part of your customer promise. During disruptions, digital channels become a continuity surface area. If they fail—or if they’re not governed and observable—you don’t just lose deflection. You lose access. Continuity is an enterprise outcome: Customers stay informed and can self-serve when appropriate Urgent cases reach trained humans Agents remain safe, connected, and supported Operations maintain integrity even when dependencies wobble “We consistently see that proactive incident communications can significantly reduce customer anxiety and help manage volume.” Lou Corbeil, NiCE General Manager, Platform Operations How: A layered safeguards model for contact center BCDR Lou Corbeil’s recommendations in Contact Center Pipeline can be translated into a practical executive blueprint: layer your safeguards across customer journeys, AI + human failover, cyber resilience, workforce protection, and third-party readiness. 1. Start with customer journeys by mapping failure modes to recovery goals Most continuity plans start with systems. High-performing continuity starts with journeys . Map your critical customer journeys to potential failure modes (channel outage, knowledge unavailability, identity verification disruption, payment system latency, workforce unavailability). Then set recovery goals that match business risk—not generic uptime targets. This is also where you define what “continuity” means in operational terms: Which journeys must remain available under all circumstances? Which can degrade gracefully with alternative paths? What’s the acceptable recovery time for each tier? Corbeil’s guidance is direct: align recovery goals with the right levels of resiliency, and design orchestration so routine inquiries can be absorbed digitally while urgent cases reach trained agents. 2. Orchestrate AI and human failover intentionally, not improvisationally A continuity plan that assumes “agents will handle it” fails when agents can’t log in, evacuate, or lose connectivity. A modern plan treats automation and AI as the first line of continuity, with clear escalation paths to humans for exceptions and high-risk situations. That orchestration includes: Pre-approved “disruption flows” for digital self-service Dynamic routing policies that prioritize urgency, vulnerability, and value Knowledge governance to ensure customers receive accurate, up-to-date guidance Clear fallbacks when automation confidence drops 3. Make incident communication a core workflow, not an ad hoc scramble In disruption conditions, demand is shaped by one question: “Do customers know what’s happening?” Proactive communications reduce anxiety and can materially reduce inbound surges—because uncertainty generates contacts. Corbeil’s point is operational: incident communications are a volume-management lever. Executive-ready practice looks like: Single source of truth for status updates Predefined templates and approval paths Segmented messaging by customer impact level Coordinated agent guidance so the human and digital stories match 4. Treat remote and hybrid staffing as resilience architecture — not a policy debate Corbeil frames a useful tension: organizations may be returning to office, but should they “RTO” their contact centers given rising disaster risk? His answer: many are moving toward hybrid or distributed models to hedge localized disruptions. The strategic takeaway isn’t “remote vs office.” It’s distribution vs. concentration. Spreading operations across regions reduces reliance on a single site. Secure remote agent capabilities to keep productivity viable from anywhere. A blended model, or regional backups plus partial remote staffing, offers stronger protection. But hybrid continuity only works if intentionally engineered: Secure remote access standards Protected devices and consistent endpoint policy Backup connectivity guidance for remote staff Clearly documented agent procedures (what to do, where to go, how to connect) 5. Harden cyber resilience with controls, audits, and monitoring Continuity depends on trust. Trust depends on security. Corbeil calls out the need to harden cyber resilience through robust controls, audits, and monitoring. And DBIR data reinforces why workforce enablement and security governance belong in the same continuity conversation: the human element appears in most breaches. Continuity leaders should ensure that “secure by design” applies equally to: Identity and access controls for distributed staff Device posture and endpoint protections Third-party access and vendor risk management Incident response handoffs between security and CX operations 6. Engineer for dependency failure — vendors, telecom, and capacity overflow Many organizations have a plan that’s not tested. Corbeil points to common gaps: minimal end-to-end testing, incomplete vendor dependency management, uneven remote agent protections, and underinvestment in overflow capacity or site redundancy. This is where continuity becomes an enterprise governance issue: Do you know your single points of failure across carriers and vendors? Have you simulated partial outages and demand spikes with your partners? Do all sites meet the same resilience and security standards? 7. Drill like you mean it — and expand governance to include AI Regular drills and joint practice exercises matter because paper plans don’t reveal operational friction. Corbeil emphasizes simulated high demand and partial outages with vendors to expose weak links before customers do. Just as important: governance must now include automated systems. As enterprises increase AI-driven self-service, continuity planning must include observability and governance of automation to ensure consistent access during crises. Make AI visible: What AI should see, why it should act, how it should adapt Enterprise buyers are rightfully skeptical of vague “AI-powered” claims. In continuity, CX AI value is concrete when it’s observable. What AI should see Early signals of disruption (status events, carrier degradation, weather alerts, security signals) Demand shifts (intent spikes like “cancellation,” “outage,” “delay,” “refund”) Customer emotion and risk (sentiment, vulnerability cues, escalation probability) Operational health (queue depth, handle time drift, staffing availability, bot containment) Why AI should act To keep routine demand from collapsing human capacity To protect customers from inconsistent or outdated guidance To ensure urgent, high-risk contacts route to the right humans fast How AI should adapt Shift channel mix: increase digital containment for low-risk intents Update guidance: propagate a single approved incident narrative to bots and agents Reroute intelligently: prioritize critical intents and vulnerable customers Detect failures: flag when automation confidence drops and escalate to humans This is where unified intelligence becomes practical. Without shared context across channels, your automation can’t coordinate with your agents—and your continuity effort becomes fragmented when you most need coherence. Continuity requires unified CX AI — not siloed tools and disconnected playbooks Corbeil’s throughline is integration: business continuity becomes possible when technology, governance, and human safety operate as one system. That’s the platform differentiator. A unified CX AI platform enables continuity because it can: Orchestrate digital and human pathways from the same source of truth Apply consistent policies across channels, regions, and teams Keep incident communication aligned across bots, knowledge, routing, and agent guidance Deliver observability into automation performance and risk during the event—not after Continuity is no longer a deflection rate environment. It’s the ability to reconfigure service in real time while maintaining governance. Assess your continuity readiness with NiCE’s business continuity and disaster recovery (BCDR) white paper outlining a structured approach. Frequently Asked Questions Disaster recovery focuses on restoring specific systems or infrastructure after a failure, such as bringing a telecom carrier or platform back online, while business continuity is the broader discipline of keeping customer-facing service running throughout a disruption, including staffing, communications, and AI/human failover. In a contact center, disaster recovery is typically one component nested inside a larger business continuity and disaster recovery (BCDR) strategy that also governs journeys, workforce safety, and vendor dependencies. While downtime costs vary by industry and channel mix, IBM's 2025 data breach research puts the global average cost of a breach-related disruption at $4.4 million, and that figure doesn't capture the compounding cost of lost customer trust, abandoned self-service journeys, or agent attrition during prolonged incidents. Contact centers should model cost as the downstream cost of eroded confidence in digital channels. A modern why business continuity and disaster recovery (BCDR) plan should map critical customer journeys to failure modes and recovery time objectives, define AI-to-human escalation and orchestration rules, establish a single source of truth for incident communications, document secure remote and hybrid staffing procedures, harden identity and vendor access controls, and schedule regular joint drills with vendors to test overflow capacity. Treating these as five interlocking layers, rather than a static document, is what separates a tested plan. Yes, when properly governed: AI and automation can absorb routine, low-risk inquiries during a disruption so human agents are freed to handle urgent, emotionally charged, or high-value cases, but this only works if the organization has pre-approved "disruption flows," dynamic routing by urgency and vulnerability, and clear fallback rules for when automation confidence drops. Without observability into bot performance during the event itself, AI can just as easily propagate outdated guidance and worsen the incident. Distributing agents across regions or enabling secure remote work reduces reliance on any single site, so a localized event like a storm or power outage doesn't take down the entire operation, whereas fully centralized office models concentrate that risk in one place. The tradeoff is that hybrid resilience only holds up if it's engineered deliberately, with secure remote access standards, protected endpoints, backup connectivity, and documented procedures agents can follow under pressure. There's no universal cadence, but the article's guidance points to regular, recurring drills, ideally simulating high demand and partial outages jointly with vendors, since Corbeil notes that common gaps include minimal end-to-end testing and undertested vendor dependencies. The practical signal that a plan needs testing more often is whether it has ever been exercised outside of a real crisis. title: List of Forms and Contact Details Required to Request Medical Records in Atlanta (PI Lawyers' 2026 Checklist)
summary: The 2026 checklist of HIPAA authorization elements, Atlanta hospital contacts, and Georgia fee rules PI lawyers need to request medical records, plus how Codes Health returns complete records in a couple of weeks on a flat fee.
body_text: Atlanta personal injury lawyers lose weeks, sometimes months, chasing medical records through phone trees, fax machines, and unresponsive HIM departments. This checklist covers the authorization elements, hospital contacts, Georgia fee schedules, and submission procedures for retrieving complete records from Atlanta's major healthcare systems. For firms that want to get the chasing off their plate, platforms like Codes Health work toward complete, organized records in a couple of weeks through AI-assisted validation and persistent provider follow-up. Key Takeaways Under O.C.G.A. § 31-33-3, Georgia providers subject to the statute generally must furnish records within 30 days of the request or receipt of required payment, whichever is later. Manual retrieval can still take weeks or months HIPAA separately requires covered entities to act on an individual's right-of-access request within 30 days, subject to one limited extension. Attorney-initiated authorization requests do not automatically qualify, and state deadlines may be shorter Atlanta's four major health systems, Piedmont, Wellstar, Emory, and Grady, each run distinct submission procedures affecting processing speed Georgia's fee schedule effective July 1, 2026 caps search and retrieval at $25.88, certification at $9.70, and per-page charges from $0.97 down to $0.66, though federal restrictions can preempt these on qualifying access requests Codes Health identifies incomplete or defective authorizations as a leading cause of avoidable rejections, and its AI review catches those errors before submission Codes Health's AI platform works toward organized records in a couple of weeks on a flat fee, and firms using Filevine can submit and track requests directly inside their case files Understanding the Foundation: Your HIPAA Authorization Form for Atlanta Medical Records Most records requests from a PI firm begin with a properly executed HIPAA authorization. Under O.C.G.A. § 31-33-3, Georgia providers subject to the statute generally must furnish records within 30 days of the request or receipt of required payment, whichever is later. Keep that separate from the federal rule. HIPAA requires a covered entity to act on an individual's right-of-access request within 30 days, with one permitted extension of up to 30 additional days on timely written notice. HHS distinguishes that from a third party, such as a law firm, making its own disclosure request under an authorization, which does not carry the same timeliness requirement. Building a calendar on the assumption that every attorney request gets a federal 30 day clock leaves you exposed. Key Elements to Include in Your Authorization An authorization must contain all core elements and required statements under 45 C.F.R. § 164.508, including: Patient identification : enough for the provider to locate the chart, typically full legal name and date of birth. A Social Security number is not a HIPAA requirement, though providers may ask for identifiers beyond the statutory minimum Provider information : the specific facility name and address releasing records Authorized recipient : your firm's name, address, and contact information Specific information disclosed : a meaningful description of what is released, such as treatment notes, billing, imaging, and labs Date range : the dates or records sought, as precisely as practicable Purpose of disclosure : for example, legal representation in a personal injury matter. HHS notes that when the individual initiates the authorization, "at the request of the individual" satisfies this element Expiration : a date or qualifying expiration event consistent with HIPAA and the provider's form Patient signature and date : the patient or authorized representative signs and dates. Check the provider's current form for specific instructions Required statements : notice of the right to revoke, whether treatment or payment can be conditioned on the authorization, and potential redisclosure Specially protected records need extra attention : Psychotherapy notes are subject to special HIPAA rules and generally require a distinct authorization, which may generally only be combined with another psychotherapy-notes authorization Records subject to 42 C.F.R. Part 2 may require a Part 2-compliant consent containing the elements required by current federal regulations, including electronic-signature provisions where applicable law permits them Georgia separately restricts disclosure of certain HIV-related confidential information. Review O.C.G.A. § 24-12-21 and the provider's current requirements Treating these as checkboxes on a generic form is how requests come back unfulfilled weeks later. Utilizing E-Signature for Faster Authorization Most Atlanta providers accept electronic signatures. Codes Health provides a HIPAA-compliant e-signature workflow built for authorization forms, removing the print, sign, and scan cycle from intake. Atlanta Provider Contacts: Key Hospitals and Clinics for Medical Record Requests Grady Health System Contact Information : Address: 80 Jesse Hill Jr. Drive SE, Atlanta, GA 30303 Medical Records Phone: (404) 616-4282 Medical Records Fax: (404) 489-6447 MyChart Support: (404) 616-5551 Privacy Office: (404) 616-1706 Hours: Monday to Friday, 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM Location: Ground Floor, Patient Service Center, Room GA100 Submission Methods : The online portal at gradyhealth.org is generally fastest, then MyChart, fax with photo ID and a signed release, then mail. Special Requirements : Grady does not accept record requests by phone, and subpoenas or discovery requests must be submitted in writing rather than electronically. For the mail and fax workflow, Grady invoices after processing and releases records once the invoice is paid. Piedmont Healthcare System Piedmont's July 2026 materials identify a 28-hospital system, including Piedmont Atlanta, Fayette, and Henry. Contact Information : Piedmont Atlanta Hospital: (404) 605-5000 Piedmont Fayette Hospital: (770) 719-7000 Piedmont Henry Hospital: (678) 604-1000 Email: recordsrequest@piedmont.org System-Wide Submission : Requests can be submitted through Piedmont's Datavant e-request portal Patients can separately use the Sharing Hub feature inside Piedmont MyChart, which is not the same as the Datavant e-request option Email to recordsrequest@piedmont.org, naming the specific hospital in the subject line Fax to the facility-specific HIM department Wellstar Health System Wellstar's hospital footprint is changing, with another Columbia County hospital scheduled to open in August 2026, so check the current directory rather than a fixed count. The system uses a centralized release-of-information process. Contact Information : System Main Phone: (770) 810-8880 System Fax: (770) 810-4193 Email: ROI_EPIC@wellstar.org Wellstar Kennestone Medical Records Direct: (770) 793-5328 Wellstar Cobb Hospital: (770) 732-4000 Wellstar Douglas Medical Center: (470) 644-6000 Hours: Monday to Friday, 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM Submission Methods : Start with Wellstar's official online request process. MyChart is available to enrolled patients, and mail should be marked "ATTN: HIM Release of Information." Processing Time : Wellstar states an average turnaround of 7 to 10 business days, while noting requests may take up to 30 days. Emory Healthcare Emory operates 11 hospitals with more than 2,600 licensed beds across metro Atlanta. Contact Information : Release of Information Call Center: (404) 712-4111 Processing Time: Emory says requests generally take 7 to 10 business days after receipt, longer if the record requires updating Fees: Emory says copies requested by patients are free. Fees may apply to attorney and other non-patient requests Submission Methods : the electronic request portal at emoryhealthcare.org is generally fastest. Select the specific Emory facility from the dropdown, or fax and mail to facility-specific HIM departments. Special Requirements : a completed ROI authorization form is required. Emory also states that if a request covers multiple Emory facilities, one receiving facility can forward it to the others identified in it, which saves filing parallel requests inside that system. Additional Atlanta Facilities Northside Hospital Atlanta : MRO Service Phone: (610) 994-7500 Email: ROIRequest@northside.com Tracking: ROILog online with a tracking code Processing Time: Northside says this varies by file size, record location, and information requested Children's Healthcare of Atlanta : Release of Information: (404) 785-2431 Fax: (404) 785-9060 Email: HISROITeam@choa.org Facilities: Arthur M. Blank Hospital, Scottish Rite, Egleston Processing Time: Children's says most records arrive in 7 to 10 business days, though a request may take up to 30 days depending on complexity Special Requirements: A parent or legal guardian must sign for minors. Radiology images follow a separate request process, so review Children's current instructions rather than assuming imaging travels with the chart Atlanta VA Healthcare System : Address: 1670 Clairmont Road, Decatur, GA 30033 Phone: (404) 321-6111 Release of Information Room: GB107 Processing Time: Up to 20 business days Forms: a patient requesting their own VA records uses VA Form 10-5345a. For a patient authorizing release to a law firm or other third party, review VA Form 10-5345 and current VA instructions The Retrieval Process: Step-by-Step Guide for Atlanta PI Cases Week 1: Initial Submission Days 1 to 2: Authorization Execution Execute the HIPAA authorization at client intake Build a provider list covering every Atlanta facility involved Collect any records, bills, or explanation of benefits statements the client has Verify demographic information matches exactly across every document Days 3 to 4: Request Preparation Create a tracking log capturing provider, contact, submission date and method, follow-up date, and status Confirm current contacts for each facility, since fax numbers and direct lines change Estimate fees using Georgia's statutory rates where they apply Day 5: Batch Submission Submit each request through the most efficient method that facility accepts Save every confirmation, including fax and email receipts and mail tracking Set follow-up reminders rather than waiting for a provider to volunteer a status Weeks 2 to 4: Follow-Up and Receipt Day 7 : first follow-up wave, calling each provider to confirm receipt Day 14 : second follow-up for non-responsive providers, in writing Day 30 : accountability check against whichever timing rule applies This cadence is an internal practice recommendation, not a statutory timetable, since attorney authorization requests and individual access requests are governed differently. Georgia Fee Schedule: What Atlanta Providers Can Legally Charge Georgia's fee schedule, effective July 1, 2026, sets these maximums: Search, Retrieval and Admin: $25.88 per request Certification Fee: $9.70 per record Pages 1 to 20: $0.97 per page Pages 21 to 100: $0.83 per page Pages 101 and up: $0.66 per page The Georgia Department of Community Health warns that these state rates should not simply be applied to an individual's HIPAA access request, where federal fee restrictions can preempt them. What That Adds Up To A 500-page paper record could reach roughly $385 if the maximum search, retrieval, copying, and certification charges all apply. Without certification, it runs closer to $376, so check whether certification is actually being charged before accepting an invoice at face value. Electronic delivery can reduce cost and handling, but do not assume a $6.50 cap applies to an attorney-initiated request. HHS says covered entities may elect a flat fee of no more than $6.50 for an electronic copy of PHI maintained electronically when fulfilling an individual's access request, or may instead calculate actual allowable costs or use an average cost methodology. That option is not a universal cap. Treatment depends on whether the request qualifies as an individual's right-of-access request or is a separate third-party disclosure, and HHS distinguishes a patient directing records to a third party from a third party requesting under an authorization. Common Rejection Reasons and How to Avoid Them Codes Health identifies incomplete or defective authorizations as a leading cause of avoidable rejections in its retrieval workflow. A defective authorization forces resubmission and substantially delays the applicable processing period. Frequent rejection reasons : Missing signature or date : complete every field and verify both are present Blurry or expired photo ID : include a clear copy of current government identification where required Insufficient patient identifiers : include full name plus date of birth and dates of service Improper representative authorization : include the death certificate and representative documentation for deceased patients Expired authorization : include a specific expiration date or qualifying event Wrong department : address requests to Health Information Management, not a general line Codes Health catches these errors before submission, automatically flagging misspellings, missing dates of service, and signature issues that would otherwise cause provider rejections. Optimizing Your Workflow: Technology Solutions for Atlanta PI Lawyers The Manual Process Problem A typical car accident case involves 5 to 10 providers. A catastrophic injury case might require records from more than 30 sources. Managing that many follow-ups on top of a full caseload is where deadlines slip and files end up incomplete. Codes Health: AI-Powered Retrieval for Legal Teams Codes Health combines AI-assisted automation with human verification, working toward complete records in a couple of weeks. Platform capabilities include: AI request validation catching authorization errors before submission Persistent provider follow-up across calls, faxes, emails, and portals Completeness verification confirming records match the request before delivery Chronological organization across all providers, ready for attorney and expert review Missing Record Review surfacing gaps in treatment documentation A note on speed claims : Codes Health notes that services advertising same-day retrieval often return only the records immediately available electronically. That leaves the rest of the chart outstanding, pushes the chasing back onto your client, and, per Codes Health, contributes to churn. Codes Health does not offer same-day delivery, and works toward the complete set in a couple of weeks. A note on general AI tools : general AI platforms like ChatGPT are not designed for litigation-grade medical record review, and are not built for end-to-end retrieval, request validation, or completeness workflows. Codes Health is purpose-built for retrieval and review in plaintiff litigation, including personal injury, mass tort, and medical malpractice matters, and combines those functions in one platform. Codes Health's MIT-educated engineering team continuously builds out additional workflows and products, so the platform keeps evolving, improving, and becoming more comprehensive to meet the changing demands of modern legal practices. Pricing is a flat fee, keeping cost predictable across a caseload. Filevine Integration: Retrieval Without Leaving Your Case File For firms using Filevine case management, an embedded integration lets you: Submit medical record requests from the relevant Filevine project Track request status in real time without switching platforms Communicate with the Codes Health team inside the case workflow Receive completed medical records, billing, and imaging in the Filevine project The Filevine Codes Health partnership goes beyond a standard third-party integration, embedding retrieval inside the case-management environment your team already uses. For high-volume firms, Codes Health can also build custom integrations with CRM platforms and other medical software. Ensuring Completeness: Verifying Your Atlanta Medical Records Receiving records is only half the battle. Before closing a retrieval request: Verify date ranges : all requested dates covered without gaps Check record types : treatment notes, billing, imaging, and labs all included Confirm imaging delivery : actual images enclosed, not just radiology reports Review for legibility : no cutoff pages or unreadable sections Match to billing : services billed should appear in treatment notes Codes Health verifies completeness against the original request and works with facilities to resolve gaps before returning records to your firm. The Bottom Line for Atlanta PI Firms Most records delays in an Atlanta practice are not bad luck. They are preventable failure modes that repeat until the process changes. The first is the deadline assumption, where a calendar gets built on a federal 30 day clock that does not apply to an attorney authorization request, or on Georgia's rule without accounting for the payment trigger. The second is the fee assumption, where a firm budgets $6.50 for an electronic copy and gets an invoice several hundred dollars higher because the request was never an access request. The third is the routing error, where a request goes to a general line or a radiology fax instead of the release-of-information desk and never enters the queue. The fourth is mistaking delivery for completeness, which surfaces in trial prep when the imaging or billing file turns out never to have arrived. Each is fixable before it costs you a month. Confirm which timing and fee rule governs the request you are sending. Verify the release-of-information contact rather than the main number. Validate the authorization against provider-specific requirements before submission rather than after rejection. And check what came back against what you asked for. Codes Health is built around those checkpoints: AI validation before the request goes out, persistent follow-up while it is pending, and completeness verification before anything reaches your firm. Complete records in a couple of weeks, for a flat fee, with the chronology already done. Schedule a demonstration to see how Codes Health handles Atlanta records retrieval for your caseload. Frequently Asked Questions How long do Georgia providers have to release medical records? Under O.C.G.A. § 31-33-3, providers subject to the statute generally must furnish records within 30 days of the request or receipt of required payment, whichever is later. That is separate from HIPAA, which requires covered entities to act on an individual's right-of-access request within 30 days with one limited extension. Attorney-initiated authorization requests do not automatically qualify. In practice, manual retrieval can take weeks or months. Can I use a single HIPAA authorization to request records from multiple Atlanta providers? Provider policies vary. Emory states that if a request identifies multiple Emory facilities, one receiving facility can forward it to the others, and Piedmont accepts requests across its network through its Datavant portal. Outside a single system, expect to submit a separate authorization to each provider. What are the common reasons for medical record request rejections in Georgia? Codes Health identifies incomplete or defective authorizations as a leading cause of avoidable rejections: missing signatures or dates, inadequate photo identification where required, insufficient identifying information, and improper representative documentation for deceased patients. A defective authorization forces resubmission and delays the applicable processing period, which is why pre-submission validation matters more than fast follow-up. How can I track the status of medical record requests across different Atlanta providers? Keep a tracking log capturing provider name, contact information, submission date and method, follow-up dates, status, received date, and issues encountered. Alternatively, Codes Health provides real-time status tracking through a single interface, with visibility into each fax, call, and provider interaction. What is the difference between a HIPAA authorization and a medical records release form? A HIPAA authorization is the federally required document permitting disclosure of protected health information. A medical records release form is the broader category, covering HIPAA authorizations plus provider-specific forms. For Atlanta PI cases, use an authorization that satisfies 45 C.F.R. § 164.508 and the relevant Georgia requirements. Many Atlanta hospitals accept a standard HIPAA form, while others process their own templates faster.

title: Pucker Up, Party People: BeatBox Launches Xtreme Sour Black Cherry

body_text: August 7, 2026 – Austin, TX– BeatBox Beverages is bringing a bold new twist to the party with the launch of Xtreme Sour Black Cherry , a limited-time flavor created for fans who crave unexpected taste experiences. The newest addition to the BeatBox lineup starts with a rush of juicy, jammy cherry flavor before delivering a punch of Xtreme sourness that takes taste buds straight into party mode. This launch is all about pushing flavor further and creating a taste experience that’s impossible to ignore.” Inspired by growing consumer demand for intense flavor profiles, Xtreme Sour Black Cherry represents the latest example of BeatBox's fan-first approach to innovation. We cover this event (well, events) more than any other, particularly the auctions, with previews, news from the ground, and post-Monterey analysis. There are a few reasons for that. First, the vehicles filling the consignment lists at the Monterey auctions (there are five sales this year) are some of the rarest, most historically significant, and most valuable automobiles sold anywhere in the world all year. Price records routinely break here, and Monterey is the only auction event where we can see multiple eight-figure cars cross the block and be able to gauge their performance against expectations. Among the most anticipated this year are a Ferrari 250 P , a McLaren F1 GTR , and multiple Ferrari Enzos . Arguably the two most significant cars on offer this year are home-grown American racers—a Chevrolet Corvette Grand Sport and a Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe . Neither model has been seen at auction since 2009. In addition to those heavy-hitters, there are dozens of other rare and significant prewar greats, vintage racing and sports cars, and modern exotics crossing the block this week. Early projections suggest that this year’s sales totals may hit half a billion dollars for the first time ever in Monterey, and that this would mostly be due to more seven- and eight-figure cars being consigned in 2026 than any broad growth in the market or an overall increase in the number of vehicles offered. If there is to be any pullback or pause at the top of the market, it will be evident this week in Monterey first. Keep an eye on this post as the week develops. title: What Liveness Detection Actually Proves and Why Identity Security Needs More
summary: Learn what liveness detection proves, what it misses, and why layered identity assurance is essential against deepfakes and identity fraud.
body_text: As more identity interactions move online, organizations need to establish not only whether a face matches an identity, but whether a real person is present during capture. Liveness detection helps answer that question by identifying signs that biometric data comes from a living person rather than a photograph, replayed video, mask or synthetic representation. But it does not, by itself, prove that the person owns the claimed identity, that the capture process is secure or that the wider transaction is legitimate. That is why businesses should treat liveness detection as one layer of identity assurance and not as a complete defense against identity fraud. The question is no longer simply, “Is this a live person?” It is, “Can we trust the person, the identity evidence, the capture process and the transaction?” What is Liveness Detection? Liveness detection is a security capability used in biometric systems to determine whether a biometric sample is being captured from a present, living person rather than from an artificial representation. In a facial verification process, for example, liveness technology may analyze an image or video for signals that indicate the presence of a real person. Its purpose is to help prevent an attacker from passing a photograph, video, mask, or other imitation to a biometric system. Liveness detection is closely related to presentation attack detection, often abbreviated as PAD. Presentation attack detection focuses on identifying attempts to interfere with a biometric capture by presenting an artifact or altered biometric characteristic to a sensor. In simple terms, liveness detection helps answer: Is a real, living person present at the point of capture? That is different from several other questions involved in identity verification, including: Biometric matching: Asks whether the person’s face, fingerprint or other characteristic resembles a trusted reference Document verification: Asks whether an identity document appears to be authentic and whether its information is consistent Device and session analysis: Asks whether the interaction is taking place through a trusted device, connection, and application environment Fraud analytics: Asks whether the wider behavior or transaction appears suspicious These controls are related, but they are not interchangeable. A strong facial match does not necessarily mean that the sample was captured from a live person. Equally, a successful liveness result does not prove that the person is using their own identity. Why Liveness Detection is Important Remote identity verification was already expanding before generative AI became widely accessible. People now open accounts, access services, sit examinations, onboard for employment, and recover credentials without appearing in person. This shift has created significant benefits for businesses and consumers. It has also created new opportunities for fraud. An attacker may attempt to fool a biometric system by holding up a printed photograph, displaying an image on another device, replaying a video, or using a mask. More sophisticated attacks may involve manipulated video, synthetic faces, or digitally altered biometric data. The increasing quality of generative AI has made the difference between genuine and manipulated media harder for people to judge visually. It has also made it more important for organizations to validate how identity evidence was captured, rather than trusting what the image appears to show. A realistic face is not the same as a trustworthy identity interaction. Liveness detection helps businesses establish whether there is evidence of a real human presence. That makes it an important defense against many forms of impersonation and presentation attacks. However, its effectiveness depends on the type of attack, the quality of the implementation, the capture environment, and the way the technology is combined with other controls. What Attacks Can Liveness Detection Help Identify? Liveness detection may help identify several common attack methods. These can include: Printed photographs placed in front of a camera Facial images displayed on a phone, tablet, or monitor Replayed video recordings Two-dimensional or three-dimensional masks Images that have been altered to imitate another person Certain forms of synthetic or deepfake media presented during capture The phrase “help identify” is important. No single liveness technology should be assumed to detect every attack under every condition. Attack methods continue to change, and the performance of a system can vary according to factors such as camera quality, lighting, compression, device type, and the sophistication of the artifact being used. Organizations should be cautious when a solution is described simply as “deepfake-proof” or “fraud-proof.” Security is not a permanent state achieved through one feature. It is an ongoing process of understanding the threat environment, testing controls, and adapting as attack techniques evolve. What Liveness Detection Does Not Prove Liveness detection provides a valuable security signal, but that signal has limits. A successful liveness result does not necessarily prove that: The person is the legitimate owner of the claimed identity The identity document being used is genuine The person has permission to access the account or service The biometric data has not been manipulated elsewhere in the capture process The device or application is trustworthy The person is acting voluntarily rather than under coercion The transaction itself is legitimate The same result would be produced across every device, demographic group, or operating environment Consider a fraudster who is physically present and attempting to open an account using a stolen identity document. The fraudster may be entirely real and alive. A liveness system could correctly determine that a live person is present while the overall identity claim remains fraudulent. This is why a live face should not be confused with a verified identity. A live face is an important security signal, but it’s not a complete identity decision. Presentation Attacks and Injection Attacks are Different Problems One of the most important distinctions in modern biometric security is the difference between a presentation attack and an injection attack. A presentation attack takes place at the point of capture. An attacker presents an image, video, mask, or other artifact to the camera or biometric sensor. An injection attack occurs when fraudulent, altered, or synthetic data is introduced into the digital capture pipeline. Instead of showing a fake image to the camera, the attacker may attempt to replace the camera feed, insert prerecorded media, or manipulate the information sent to the biometric system. This distinction has significant implications. A liveness capability designed primarily to analyze what is visible in front of a camera may not, by itself, detect manipulation occurring elsewhere in the application or data stream. Organizations need to examine both the biometric sample and the integrity of the capture process. They should ask not only whether the person appears live, but also whether the biometric data came from the expected camera, device, and session without unauthorized substitution. This is particularly important as deepfake technology becomes more accessible. A synthetic face might be presented on a screen, but it might also be introduced digitally in a way that bypasses a conventional camera-based check. Passive and Active Liveness Detection Liveness detection is commonly described as either passive or active. Passive liveness detection generally evaluates a biometric capture without asking the user to perform a specific action. From the user’s perspective, the process may feel like taking an ordinary selfie or looking into a camera. Active liveness detection asks the user to complete a challenge. This could involve turning their head, blinking, speaking, following an object on the screen or performing another instructed action. Both approaches can provide value. Passive liveness can reduce friction and make the verification experience faster and more accessible. This may be particularly important in high-volume consumer environments where abandonment has a direct commercial cost. Active liveness can introduce an explicit challenge-and-response step, providing another signal that the interaction is happening in real time. However, neither label indicates security quality on its own. A passive system is not automatically less secure, and an active system is not automatically more secure. The appropriate method depends on the use case, threat model, user population, operating environment, and level of risk. The relevant questions are: Which attacks has the technology been designed to detect? How has it been tested? Under which conditions was it evaluated? What happens when the system is uncertain? How does the control affect legitimate users? How is its performance monitored as attacks evolve? How Should Businesses Evaluate Liveness Technology? Businesses should look beyond broad accuracy claims and ask for evidence that reflects their intended deployment. Useful questions include: Which presentation attacks were included in testing? How does the system address digitally injected media? Was the technology evaluated by an independent testing organization? Does the testing reflect the devices and environments used by real customers? How are false rejections balanced against the acceptance of attacks? How does performance vary across lighting conditions and camera types? How has the organization evaluated demographic performance? Can security thresholds be adjusted according to transaction risk? How frequently is the technology updated as new attack methods emerge? What evidence is available beyond a single summary score or certification? Standards and independent assessments can provide valuable evidence, particularly when they offer clarity about the testing methodology and attack types used. However, a test result for one component should not be interpreted as proof that an entire identity system is secure. A biometric control may perform well in a laboratory and still be weakened by poor application security, an unprotected capture channel, inappropriate thresholds or weak processes elsewhere in the identity journey. Businesses need to evaluate the system as it will actually be deployed. The Future of Identity Assurance is Bigger Than Liveness Liveness detection will remain an essential part of remote identity verification. As more interactions move online and synthetic media becomes more convincing, establishing genuine human presence will become even more important. But the industry must resist the temptation to turn liveness into a shorthand for complete identity security. The organizations best prepared for the next generation of identity fraud will be those that evaluate the complete chain of trust. They will combine proof of presence with proof of identity, capture integrity, contextual risk analysis and appropriate escalation. The most useful question for business leaders is not, “Do we have liveness detection?” It is: “What evidence do we have that this person, identity, device, capture process and transaction can be trusted together?” That is the standard modern identity security must meet.

POS Purchase Meaning: Point-of-Sale Transactions Explained
summary: What does POS purchase mean? This guide explains what a POS purchase is, how it works, what it looks like on your bank statement, and why it matters for restaurant operators.
body_text: A POS purchase is a transaction completed through a point-of-sale system. On a bank statement, “POS purchase” generally means a card was used to pay a merchant rather than withdraw cash or transfer money between accounts. In restaurants, a POS purchase can happen at a counter, tableside, at a self-service kiosk, or through an online ordering channel. Toast’s restaurant POS system brings these orders and payments into one platform, helping operators keep transaction data connected across their business. This guide explains what a POS purchase means, how it compares with other transaction types, and how each type of POS purchase works. Key takeaways A POS purchase is a point-of-sale transaction that usually appears on a bank statement as a card payment to a merchant. POS purchases can happen by card, contactless wallet, handheld device, self-service kiosk, or integrated online ordering. Card purchases are authorized at checkout and settled later, so they may appear as pending first. Unrecognized POS purchases should be checked against receipts and reported to the card provider if they remain unfamiliar. RESOURCE Restaurant POS Comparison Tool A free, customizable Restaurant POS Comparison Tool to research and compare point of sale systems in one Excel spreadsheet. RESOURCE Restaurant POS Comparison Tool A free, customizable Restaurant POS Comparison Tool to research and compare point of sale systems in one Excel spreadsheet. What does POS purchase mean? POS stands for “point of sale,” meaning the place or system where a customer completes a purchase. A POS purchase is the individual transaction. If a guest orders a burger and pays by card, that payment is a POS purchase. A POS system is the technology used to accept and record the transaction. It can include hardware, payment processing, order-management software, and connections to restaurant reporting and operational tools. In a restaurant, POS purchases can happen in several places. A guest might insert a card at the counter, tap a mobile wallet at the table, or order and pay through a self-service kiosk. Each is a POS purchase, even though the device and payment method are different. POS purchases compared with other transaction types POS purchases are one of several transaction types that may appear in a bank account or payment record, with each describing how a payment is made or processed. These categories can overlap. For example, a restaurant payment can be a POS purchase, a card-present transaction, and a pending charge at the same time. Transaction type What it means POS purchase A purchase processed through a merchant’s point-of-sale system ATM withdrawal Cash removed from a bank account through an ATM ACH or bank transfer Money moved directly between bank accounts Card-present purchase A physical card or mobile wallet is used at the merchant Card-not-present purchase Payment details are submitted remotely, usually online or by phone Recurring payment A merchant charges the customer on a schedule Pending purchase The payment is authorized but has not fully posted Settled purchase The final transaction amount has posted to the account What does “POS purchase” mean on a bank statement? When “POS purchase” appears on a bank statement, it generally identifies a card transaction with a merchant. The exact label varies by bank, so it does not always reveal whether the customer swiped, inserted, tapped, or entered the card online. A POS purchase entry typically includes: The merchant descriptor The transaction or posting date The purchase amount A pending or completed status The merchant descriptor may show the business’s legal name, parent company, or payment-processing name instead of the name on its storefront. The displayed date can also differ from the date of the purchase because authorization and settlement happen at different stages. If you do not recognize a POS purchase, compare the amount and date with your receipts, search the displayed merchant name, and check with anyone else authorized to use the account. If the transaction still appears unauthorized, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau recommends contacting your bank or card provider immediately. Types of POS purchases POS purchases can be categorized by their payment method, device, or ordering channel. These types are not mutually exclusive. A guest could make a contactless, card-present purchase using a handheld POS device, for example. For example, Toast Payment Processing works directly with Toast POS, keeping payment and order data connected in one restaurant platform. Type How the purchase happens Card-present The customer swipes, inserts, or taps a card Contactless The customer taps a card or mobile wallet Mobile POS An employee processes the purchase on a handheld device Self-service The customer orders and pays through a kiosk Integrated online ordering A digital order flows into the restaurant’s connected POS platform 1. Card-present purchases A card-present purchase happens when the customer presents a physical card or eligible mobile wallet at the restaurant. They can swipe a card’s magnetic stripe, insert its chip, or tap a contactless card or device. These purchases are common at restaurant counters and checkout stations. The POS sends the payment information for authorization and updates the check once the purchase is approved. Toast hardware supports EMV chip cards and NFC contactless payments, giving guests several ways to pay while helping operators keep every payment tied to the correct check. 2. Contactless purchases A contactless purchase lets the customer tap a compatible card, phone, or smartwatch near the payment terminal. The devices communicate using near-field communication, or NFC. Apple Pay, Google Pay, and contactless bank cards are common examples. When the customer taps at the restaurant’s payment device, the purchase is generally treated as a card-present transaction. Contactless payments can help keep checkout simple: the guest does not have to hand over a card or insert it into the reader. 3. Mobile POS purchases A mobile POS purchase is processed through a portable device instead of a fixed terminal. Handheld POS devices are especially useful in dining rooms, patios, food trucks, stadiums, and off-site events. Toast Go 3 allows restaurant employees to take orders and accept swipe, dip, tap, and mobile payments on the same handheld device. Servers can manage the transaction close to the guest instead of moving between the table and a stationary terminal. That shorter workflow means fewer handoffs. The order enters the POS where it is taken, and the payment can be completed at the table. 4. Self-service POS purchases A self-service POS purchase lets the customer place and pay for an order without a cashier entering each item. The customer selects menu items, chooses modifiers, reviews the total, and pays through a kiosk. Toast’s Self-Ordering Kiosk connects directly with Toast POS. Orders flow from the kiosk to the restaurant’s POS and kitchen systems without staff manually entering them again. For guests, this creates more control over ordering and customization. For restaurants, it can help keep lines moving while employees focus on food preparation and hospitality. 5. Integrated online purchases An online purchase happens when the customer orders through a restaurant’s website or another digital channel. Because the physical card is not presented to the restaurant, it is usually categorized as a card-not-present transaction . However, it can still become part of the restaurant’s broader POS record. Toast Online Ordering connects digital orders with the restaurant’s POS and kitchen, allowing online and on-premise orders to move through the same platform. This connection means restaurant employees do not have to copy online orders into a separate system. Menu information, order details, and fulfillment options can remain connected across channels. How does a POS purchase work? A card purchase can appear as pending before it becomes a settled transaction. Authorization happens during checkout, while settlement happens later. Here’s how a POS system typically processes a purchase : The restaurant receives the order: An employee enters it into the POS, or it arrives through a connected kiosk or digital ordering channel. The POS calculates the total: The system applies item prices, modifiers, discounts, taxes, service charges, and tips as appropriate. The customer chooses a payment method: Depending on the restaurant, that might be cash, a physical card, a mobile wallet, gift card, or another accepted method. The payment is submitted for authorization: For a card purchase, the payment processor sends the request through the card network to the issuing financial institution. The transaction is approved or declined: Approval confirms that the payment can proceed. It does not necessarily mean the funds have already reached the restaurant. The POS records the purchase: The system saves relevant details such as the items ordered, payment method, time, location, employee, discounts, and tip. The payment is settled: The final amount is posted and deposited according to the restaurant’s payment-processing schedule. For restaurant operators, the purchase also creates useful business data. When ordering, payments, and reporting are connected through Toast, transaction information can flow into the restaurant’s operations without staff manually reconciling separate systems. A POS purchase is more than a payment Every POS purchase can show a restaurant what sold, when it sold, how the guest paid, and where the transaction happened. Connected transaction data can support decisions about menus, staffing, inventory, guest engagement, tips, and multi-location performance. Toast Now gives operators mobile access to live sales and operational information. Toast reports that more than 35% of Toast Now users logged in at least 10 times per week during the measured period in April 2024. Toast IQ goes further by analyzing restaurant data and turning it into personalized answers, recommendations, and actions. In short, a POS purchase completes the payment. Toast helps restaurants use the information behind it. FAQ What does POS stand for? POS stands for “point of sale,” the place or system where a customer completes a purchase. What does POS purchase mean on my bank statement? A POS purchase on your bank statement generally means a card payment was processed through a merchant’s point-of-sale system. Is a POS purchase the same as a debit card purchase? Not exactly—a debit card purchase made through a merchant’s checkout is a POS purchase, but POS purchases can also use credit cards, mobile wallets, cash, or other payment methods. Can a POS purchase be disputed? Yes, an incorrect or unauthorized POS purchase can be disputed by contacting your bank or card issuer promptly. What is a POS system in a restaurant? A restaurant POS system such as Toast combines hardware and software to take orders, process payments, route orders, and record sales data in one place. How long does a POS purchase take to process? A POS purchase is authorized during checkout, but it may take several business days to settle and appear as completed, depending on the merchant, processor, and bank.
